Question: My landlord sold the house I live in. What time do I have to leave? Do I get money to move?
Answer: There is a lot of confusion about this. Under Common Law, a lease is attached to and runs with the property, not the owner. Your lease is an asset that was sold with the house. If the new owner wants to get you out, he/she has to give you proper notice, which under common law is 30 days on a month-to-month lease. Where I live (Alberta) it is 90 days on a month-to-month lease. Alberta is somewhat tenant friendly. On a longer lease, the lease expires on the original end date, but the landlord must give you 30 days notice that they are not going to renew it, otherwise it reverts to a month-to-month lease and the 30 or 90 day rule applies. Read your local landlord and tenant act to see what applies. Also read your lease to see what it says, but remember, the lease cannot override the landlord/tenant law. No, you do not get money to move. In my experience you find a friend with a pickup truck and get a few other friends to help. If you don’t have any friends, hire a moving company.

Question: How are mineral resources like oil managed to prevent issues such as a neighbor drilling and extracting resources from my land? For example, if I find oil on my property, how is it ensured that my neighbor cannot drill and take my resources?
Answer: You can drill an offset well near the property boundary and produce the oil before he does. Oil is mobile, and if you are sharing the same underground pool of it, it will flow toward his producing wells unless you drill your own wells in the pool. Alternatively, you can sign a pooling agreement to share the revenue from his wells, but in return you have to share the costs involved in drilling the wells. Be prepared to bring a lot of money to the negotiating table. Case in point: The Alberta provincial government sold oil leases on provincial land immediately adjacent to a national park, and oil companies started drilling them. The Canadian federal government sued the Alberta government for a share of the royalties on the grounds that some of the oil came from under the park. The judges ruled that the only way the federal government could get a share of the money was to drill wells near the boundary INSIDE the national park. It was a “use it or lose it” situation and since the federal government would not do it, it lost it. Since the provincial government was drilling oil wells in its own provincial parks, it didn’t see why the federal government couldn’t do the same in its national parks. It just disguised them to look more like trees than oil wells. Working for an oil company, I designed a computer system to identify places where we needed to drill offset wells. It located all the wells drilled by other companies immediately adjacent to our non-producing leases and got the production rates for them from our databases and government files. Then it created a list of the leases in descending order based on other companies’ nearby production, for use by the exploration department. They would go out, shoot seismic on the leases, find the pool boundaries, and decide whether or not and where to drill. This required access to information that the average Joe does not have. The damn program could even find production data for “tight holes” — wells where the information is supposed to be secret. Thats what happens when you put some artificial intelligence into a program, and it figures out what to do by itself.

Question: Why did the new light rail chose standard rail gauge 750 volt pantograph wire instead of the existing legacy streetcar system using custom rail with trolley pole 600 volt wire?

It is very flexible and can operate as anything from a tram to a light metro train, underground, elevated, but usually at grade since that is cheaper. While its rolling stock is similar to a traditional tram, it operates at a higher capacity and speed, and can be used in muliple unit mode with a variable number of vehicles from 1 to 4 or 5. Question: If chicken/beef is dried in a food dehydrator like for jerky, just meat and salt added, how long, if at all, could it be left at room temperature in a sealed bag/container?

Question: Why is Canada so green north of Edmonton? Shouldn't the rain-shadow of the Rockies make it as dry as eastern Montana?
Answer: It is because of global wind circulation patterns. This is an oversimplication, but there are three main global wind patterns, the Ferrel Cell, the Hadley Cell, and the Polar Cell in both hemispheres both north and south of the equator. The Ferrel Cell picks up moisture at about 30 degrees north and south latitude, and deposits it at the equator, which is why most of the world’s deserts are at about 30 degrees and south of the equator, and the equator is mostly tropical rain forest. The Hadley Cell picks up moisture at about 30 degrees north/south - hence deserts, and deposits it at about 60 degrees north/south. The Polar Cell picks up moisture from the poles and deposits it at about 60 degrees, too. In most of both the US and Canada, climates are driven by the Hadley Cell. If you will note, the 30th parallel runs through the US (which has some big deserts), and the 60th parallel runs through Canada, so northern Canada is much wetter then the southern US. Edmonton is at 53.5 degrees, so it only gets wetter and greener north of that. The Earth is also rotating, so the coreolis effect adds an additional complication. Winds in the Ferrel Cell region blow from east to west (the easterly trade winds), those in the Haldley Cell blow from west to east (the prevailing westerlies), and the polar easterlies blow from east to west. Since the Rocky Mountains in western Montana are very high, the prevailing westerlies drop most of their moisture on the west slopes of the Rockies, leaving the plains in eastern Montana very dry. OTOH, the Rockies west of Edmonton are much lower, so the winds drop their moisture on the very fertile farmland around Edmonton (the Parkland Belt). Further north the mountains are even lower, so the winds drop too much rain for most agriculture, and so there are a lot of green trees.
